_readme: Audit log for the obot hub site. The newest entry's version is what the header badge shows on every page, and this whole log is the modal behind the catalog's "full log" link. Newest first; dates are UTC ISO-8601. Append an entry with a semver bump for any change that alters what the site shows (see AGENTS.md, Key files). The build counts commits touching site/ and scripts/ since this file was last committed, and the badge plus the Navigator sweep both report it when that count is not zero — so an unbumped change is visible rather than silent.

changes: Whether a decision has been made now has one authority — the artifact page declares its own state next to his words, and the registry and the published index are a generated view and a checked one. Ten of twenty-one artifacts disagreed before this; the deploy now fails rather than publishing a decision log that is wrong about his own decisions (#196, #255).

The requirements count stops calling a blocked mechanism drift. Nothing can put an issue on the obot Roadmap board any more — the obotclaw App is refused on a user-owned project and the guard denies the only credential that works (#252) — so every requirement filed since joins the off-board set and the drift number climbs by itself. Those rows are now counted as blocked rather than as drift, still shown, still saying Unstaged, with one line under the table naming the block and linking the decision (#254).

The queue says it once instead of eleven times. Eleven separate "fix its stage on the board" cards, each proposing a repair no agent can perform, are replaced by a single card naming the cause — and the card that used to say an issue sits on the board with no stage now checks whether it is on the board at all, which for all eleven it was not.

The audit stops offering repairs it cannot run. 61 of 98 findings propose a board write; each now says so on the row, in the rail, in the audit fold and in the apply lane, and accepting one is refused before anything is attempted rather than failing halfway. The three ops are kept, not deleted — they work again the day #252 is answered.

The briefing's config line carries its own age once the count is more than six hours old, so last night's number cannot be read as this morning's. The count comes from a file nothing refreshes on a schedule, and the site only flagged it as stale after three days (#247).

The briefing exists, at one URL you can bookmark on your phone: /reports/briefing/. Ten lines at most, one line per item, the ask at the front, every line a link you can act on without opening anything else. It always shows current state — there are no dated briefings to catch up on, because the diary is the archive. Skip it for a week and the next one is still complete (#247, under #238).

It is a second view of the queue, not a second computation of it. The same buildItems() that ranks /roadmap.html feeds the briefing, so the two surfaces cannot disagree about what counts as waiting. What differs is that the briefing has to cut and the queue does not: release candidates and decisions carry in full, the longest-waiting of everything else gets two lines, and the rest is one counted line linking the full queue. Nothing is ever dropped silently — a ten-line page that lies by omission would be worse than the twenty-line one.
Config items appear as a count and never as text, which is the rule the local-only guard enforces rather than the rule anyone remembers.
Two things are still owed and say so on the page rather than being faked: the overnight record of what shipped, and the fold's own freshness stamp. Both arrive with the morning fold (obot.agent#202).

A requirement now says whose decision it carries (#215). Two lines at the foot of the body: who authored it, and who approved it — or the literal EMPTY, which means nobody has and is the normal, correct state for work an agent wrote. The catalog and the audit both read it.

Approved by holds a citation that resolves, never prose. A decision id (D0018.1) resolves to what was asked, what he said, the channel and the date, by joining the registry's questions to the codes each decision block says it resolves — a join nothing in the repo made before. A native GitHub review (owner/repo#123 review) resolves against the reviews API and is the preferred form where it exists, because an approval that lives on the object being approved has no relay chain to have provenance about.

The nightly audit gained APPROVAL-UNRESOLVED, which fires when a requirement claims his approval and cannot show it, and PROVENANCE-MISSING for requirements filed from 2026-08-18 with no block. Neither ever demands an approval: EMPTY passes.

The drafted-by attribution line stops asserting a review. It named the author and then added "and reviewed by @jwildfire" — on 75 of this hub's 113 requirements, none of which carry any record of that review, including #215 itself, which was drafted in an unattended session. The line now ends at the author. Those 75 bodies are counted in reports/requirement-provenance/ rather than rewritten.

The header carries a version number on every page, and it tells the truth about when the page shipped (#224). @jwildfire, 2026-08-16: "Add a version # on the hub in the header and let me hover to see when it was launched." Hover on a pointer, tap on a phone: the panel gives the launch time in ET, how long ago that was against your own clock, and the commit it was built from, linked.

The version and the launch time now come from different places, because only one of them can know. The version is this file's newest entry, which stays hand-written. The launch time and commit are stamped by the deploy itself. Before this, the badge showed this file's date as though it were the launch time: on 2026-08-16 the deployed catalog page read "v2.12.0 - 2026-08-16 01:20 EDT" on a page that was actually built at 18:15 EDT, wrong by seventeen hours, because the roadmap rebuild (#211, D0018) shipped without a changelog entry.

When the changelog falls behind what the site ships, the badge says so instead of choosing a half to believe. It is counted in commits touching site/ and scripts/ since this file was last committed, not in hours - the site redeploys on a daily cron, so an hours-based warning would grow by a day every morning on a site nobody had touched and be permanent within a week. The two machine-written artifacts are excluded.

The badge was on catalog.html and on none of the other ten published pages, including the queue that D0018 had made the front door the day before he asked where the version number was. It now comes from the shared header, and the deploy fails if any page loses it - or if any page says "local build", which is what every page would quietly say if the stamping step were ever dropped.
The Navigator sweep reports the same verdict, read from the published _site/version.json rather than computed a second time from a local clone that is routinely behind the deployed commit.

New Audit section (requirement #92): a nightly rule sweep of the roadmap's own conventions, collapsed by default, listing every finding with its evidence, a high/medium/low confidence, and a specific proposed change.

Accept and Reject on every finding. Accept opens a prefilled decision issue; the apply lane re-validates the finding against a fresh audit, then applies it — mechanical fixes as a closed vocabulary of operations, judgment calls through a bounded agent. Rejections change nothing and mute the finding for 60 days, or until its evidence changes.

New collapsed rule list: all 22 rules with what each checks, why the convention exists, how a violation is fixed, and whether the rule is firing, quiet, skipped or broken — so an empty findings list can be told apart from an audit that could not run.
